column3: Names Gardens of Eden as an enduring reward and adds their flowing rivers.
Shows the garden's inhabitants joyfully occupied, adding the lived condition within the destination.
Uses a gate as an entry threshold, but concerns a terrestrial confrontation rather than the promised garden.
Joins entry into Gardens of Eden with angels entering through every gate, directly expanding the focus's opened gates.
David's strengthened kingdom and judgment do not clarify the garden or its gates.
Presents the opened sky as many gates, a distinct threshold image without the garden destination.
Directly names entry into Gardens of Eden, their rivers, and the pious recipients' unrestricted provision.
The immediate continuation describes reclining guests calling for abundant fruit and drink within the opened garden.
Opened gates of heaven release floodwater, a different and adverse use of the opening image.
Identifies Gardens of Eden as the certain unseen promise made to the Merciful's servants.
The immediate conclusion makes the garden's provision inexhaustible.
Describes enduring gardens with rivers, purified spouses, and divine pleasure for the God-conscious.
Names Gardens of Eden as the believers' destination and adds adornment and reclining within them.
Adds abundant fruit for eating, developing the hospitality anticipated by the opened gates.
Provides a general account of eternal garden membership without clarifying Eden or its entrance.
The tightly closed household doors form a contrary, non-eschatological threshold scene.
Solomon's distraction behind a screen does not develop the promised garden or its gates.
Uses opening for manifest victory, a metaphorical access image rather than entry into Paradise.
Directly depicts the God-conscious arriving at Paradise, its gates opened, keepers greeting them, and their eternal entry.
The immediate continuation adds the matched companions awaiting the garden's guests.
A heavenly gate that deniers would explain away is a contrary access image, not the promised destination.
States the opposite outcome: arrogant deniers have neither opened heavenly gates nor entry into the garden.
The immediate shift to boiling drink and foulness establishes the contrary hospitality of the other final destination.
General divine admission of believers to rivered gardens adds little after the direct Eden passages.
The opened gates of Hell and its keepers provide a structured negative counterpart to Paradise's opened gates.
The exception for God's sincere servants only loosely supports the worthy recipients in the surrounding discourse.
Opening every gate before sudden seizure warns that opened access is not invariably divine welcome.
An opened gate of severe punishment is a contrary threshold with limited bearing on Eden.
The immediate context identifies this promised destination with the Day of Account.
Mentions gardens and palaces as possible divine gifts, without the Eden or entrance scene.
Directly names entry into Gardens of Eden and adds their adornment, though it repeats the core destination.
The declaration of clear warning does not explain the garden or its gates.
The brief phrase Gardens of Bliss confirms the setting but adds no new detail after earlier garden descriptions.
Repeats the immediately preceding bare formula Gardens of Bliss without additional value.
Commands entry through Hell's gates for eternity, furnishing a direct inverse to the focus's welcome.
Places the God-conscious in gardens and springs but lacks the Eden or gate dimension.
Hell's seven apportioned gates clarify how gates can structure judgment, as a contrast to the open garden gates.
Remembrance of the final abode in the immediate prelude supplies only broad destination context.
Uses gardens for earthly growth from blessed rain, a distinct sense from the eternal residence.
Commands the God-conscious to enter in peace on the Day of Eternity, closely paralleling admission to the focus's garden.
The immediate Hell verse supplies the opposing settled destination and its wretched lodging.
Gardens and springs describe worldly provision, not entrance into the enduring garden.
The command to give disbelievers respite has no useful connection to the focus.
Satan's expulsion does not clarify the open gates of Gardens of Eden.
Household doors and reclining couches offer a remote architectural parallel only.
The identification of Jonah as a messenger does not develop the focus.
The caravan and Joseph's scent have no connection to the promised garden threshold.
Gardens and springs again describe a worldly people's condition rather than the final abode.
Promises two gardens to one who fears standing before the Lord, adding a recipient condition to the reward.
The immediate continuation completes the varieties of Hell's punishment, sharpening the contrast in final hospitality.
A lofty garden supports the elevated blissful setting but adds no entry or Eden detail.
Directly names eternal Gardens of Eden with rivers as God's reward and mutual good pleasure.
David's duty to judge justly and warning of punishment do not clarify the focus's destination image.
Places the God-conscious in gardens and springs, reinforcing the recipient and setting without the gates.
The angels pray for the righteous and their families to be admitted to the promised Gardens of Eden.
The command to enter Hell's gates eternally is the immediate paired contrast to 39:73's open Paradise gates.
General placement of believers in Gardens of Bliss adds little beyond the established reward scene.
Promises believers enduring Gardens of Eden and good dwellings, adding residential permanence and divine pleasure.
The immediate Hell cohort receives no welcome, a pointed reversal of the garden's open, hospitable access.
Entry through a gate in prostration supplies a conditional terrestrial threshold, not the final garden.
Combines forgiveness, entry into Gardens of Eden, and good dwellings, directly elaborating the promised residence.
The opening oath by the Quran does not explain the garden-gate image.
Conditional admission to Gardens of Bliss is a generic reward statement after stronger Eden parallels.
The fire's effect on human skin has no connection to the focus.
Reclining on green cushions adds a remote detail of paradisal repose after the immediate hospitality verses.
Entering houses by their doors is an ethical terrestrial analogy with limited relevance to Paradise's gates.
Garden dwellers questioning others adds only a general feature of the afterlife setting.
The immediate dispute over the miserable resting place continues the hostile counter-hospitality of Hell.
A household door scene of pursuit and accusation is unrelated to final admission.
Prepared eternal rivered gardens restate the reward without Eden or opened gates.
The list of former factions does not develop the final garden scene.
The replacement of fertile gardens with poor produce is a worldly contrast to enduring garden abundance.
Gardens and springs characterize the secure but generic blessed setting, without an entrance dimension.
Korah's burdensome treasure keys do not clarify access to the promised garden.
Rest, fragrant provision, and a garden of bliss add a broad reception image only.
Gardens of Bliss for believing workers repeat the general reward after fuller Eden descriptions.
The angels' collective prostration does not clarify the garden or its gates.
Expulsion from worldly gardens and springs is only a distant reversal of secure residence.
Names Gardens of Firdaws as believers' lodging, adding the language of prepared hospitality.
Iblis's refusal to prostrate does not develop the focus.
Pharaoh's wife asks for a house with God in the garden, adding personal nearness and refuge to the destination.
Promises believer entry into eternal rivered gardens, purified spouses, and deep shade.
Describes the garden as an inheritance for deeds, but adds little to the gate-and-entry focus.
Abraham's request to inherit the Garden of Bliss is a general aspiration without entry detail.
Calls eternal rivered gardens a lodging from God for the God-conscious, supporting the hospitality reading.
Adds fruit and whatever the garden's people request, directly extending the provision motif.
Paradise is brought near to the God-conscious, a distinct image of access to the promised destination.
Its detailed but familiar rivered-garden reward is redundant after the earlier Eden and hospitality passages.
The absence of questioning between close friends has no useful connection to the focus.
Entry through a gate in humility offers a terrestrial access condition, not the opened gates of Eden.
Eternal garden companionship as reward is a generic restatement with no gate or Eden detail.
A demanded private orchard miracle does not illuminate the promised final garden.
The dispute over Jesus's killing and crucifixion is unrelated to the focus.
Announces eternal rivered gardens to believing men and women, but repeats the established reward formula.
Past nations' embellished deeds and painful punishment do not clarify the focus.
Paradise being brought near supplies a concise arrival image complementary to the opened gates.
The description of unaware corrupters has no connection to the focus.
Paradise is brought near to the God-conscious, closely complementing its peaceful entrance in 50:34.
Repentance leading to entry into rivered gardens adds a general path to the reward but repeats earlier material.
Faith and righteous work leading to eternal rivered gardens is a final generic restatement.
The verse immediately introduces the focus as the excellent final return prepared for the God-conscious.
The paired declaration that transgressors have the worst return frames the garden as the contrasting final destination.
Angels greet the Garden's entrants with peace, continuing the every-gate arrival scene of 13:23.
Commands the God-conscious to enter the gardens in peace and security, directly supplying the admission announced in 15:45.
Identifies the successful believers as inheritors of al-Firdaws, a direct final-destination parallel.
Makes their inheritance of al-Firdaws an eternal residence.
Shows garden dwellers and their spouses reclining in shade on couches, closely extending the focus's hospitality scene.
The greeting of peace from the Merciful adds the welcome accompanying the garden's open access.
Sets apart God's chosen servants as the recipients of the honored garden provision described in the following verses.
Names their provision as known and allotted, complementing the unfailing provision in the focus's immediate context.
Specifies fruits as the honored provision of the Garden's people.
Places the Garden's people on thrones facing one another, expanding the social hospitality within it.
The Garden's people praise God after inheriting the land and freely settling in Paradise, completing the arrival scene of 39:73.
Commands the believers and their spouses to enter Paradise in joy, directly paralleling the focus's opened entry.
Adds vessels and cups carried around the entrants, developing the garden's hospitable provision.
Places the God-conscious in a secure station, supplying the safety implied by the opened Gates of Eden.
Adds fine silk and brocade as the clothing of the secure Garden's people.
Pairs them with companions, extending the garden's prepared hospitality.
Shows them calling safely for every kind of fruit, closely matching the requestable provision in 38:51.
States that they will not taste death beyond the first death, clarifying the permanence of the destination.
Identifies this secure reward as grace from the Lord and the great success.
Addresses the Garden as the promised reward for every penitent keeper, supplying its recipients.
Defines those recipients as those who fear the Merciful unseen and come with a returning heart.
Grants the Garden's people whatever they wish and more, completing the access and provision scene of 50:31-34.
Places the God-conscious in gardens and bliss, a clear parallel to the focus's recipient and destination.
Shows them reclining on arranged couches, extending the same hospitality motif as 38:51.
Describes the two promised gardens as richly branched, adding their abundance.
Supplies two flowing springs in the gardens, developing their sustaining provision.
Adds every pair of fruit in the two gardens, complementing the focus's fruit provision.
Shows their people reclining on lined couches amid near fruit, a close hospitality parallel.
Places the foremost on inlaid thrones, developing the Garden-of-Bliss setting introduced at 56:12.
Adds chosen fruit to the Garden's provision.
Introduces the companions of the right as a distinct blessed company.
Describes them amid lote trees without thorns, adding the garden environment.
Adds abundant fruit that is neither exhausted nor forbidden.
Names the reward as a lofty garden, directly developing the elevated final residence.
Rewards patience with a garden and silk, directly identifying the final abode.
Shows its people reclining on couches in shade, extending the comfort of the garden welcome.
Describes its shade and fruit brought near for easy access.
Promises the God-conscious a success consisting of gardens and grapevines.
Places the righteous in delight, initiating a direct reward scene.
Shows them looking from couches, extending the settled hospitality of Paradise.
Commands the faithful soul to enter God's Paradise, a concise direct counterpart to the focus's open gates.
Makes believers who do righteous deeds eternal companions of the Garden.
Describes a Garden prepared for the God-conscious, directly reinforcing its intended recipients.
Rewards those who seek forgiveness with eternal rivered gardens.
Promises emigrants and strivers entry into rivered gardens as their divine reward.
Links obedience to God and His messenger with entry into eternal rivered gardens.
Promises believers and righteous workers enduring rivered gardens as a true divine promise.
Promises entry into gardens with rivers for faith, prayer, almsgiving, and support of the messengers.
Rewards truthful speech with eternal rivered gardens, adding a moral path to the destination.
Gives the truthful eternal rivered gardens alongside God's pleasure.
Names for the God-conscious a home of peace with their Lord, closely complementing safe entry to the Garden.
Makes the people of faith and righteous work the eternal companions of the Garden.
Depicts the Garden's people entering amid praise after resentment is removed and rivers flow beneath them.
Promises believers mercy, good pleasure, and gardens of lasting bliss.
Promises the foremost believers eternal rivered gardens and God's pleasure.
Guides believing righteous workers to gardens with rivers beneath them.
Places believers who humble themselves before their Lord among the eternal companions of the Garden.
Describes the garden promised to the God-conscious as eternally fruitful and shaded, contrasting the Fire's end.
States that believers and righteous workers are admitted to eternal rivered gardens by their Lord's permission.
Promises the God-conscious the good abode of the Hereafter, the best of which is their garden home.
Promises the faithful and righteous workers gardens whose reward is never lost.
Promises repentant believers entry into the Garden without diminution, immediately preparing 19:61.
Identifies the believer who comes with righteous deeds as receiving the highest ranks.
States that God admits believers and righteous workers to gardens with rivers beneath them.
Names the Garden of Eternity as the promised reward and destination of the God-conscious.
Promises believing righteous workers lofty chambers within gardens with rivers beneath them.
Makes gardens of refuge the hospitality prepared for believers and righteous workers.
Promises steadfast believers that angels will assure them of the Paradise they were promised.
Presents Paradise as the believers' welcome and provision from the Forgiving Merciful.
Places believers and righteous workers in gardens, receiving whatever they wish from their Lord.
Removes fear and grief from God's servants immediately before their entry into Paradise.
States that God will admit the believers into the Paradise He has made known to them.
States that God admits believers and righteous workers into gardens with rivers beneath them.
Describes the garden promised to the God-conscious with rivers, fruits, and forgiveness.
Promises believing men and women entry into eternal rivered gardens and the removal of their evil deeds.
Promises whoever obeys God and His messenger entry into gardens with rivers beneath them.
Calls believers to a Garden as vast as heaven and earth, prepared for faith in God and His messengers.
Promises the party of God entry into eternal rivered gardens together with His good pleasure.
